%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%% Abstract %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\begin{abstract}
Every televised match produces a flood of visual information, yet automatically identifying players, goalkeepers, referees, and the ball still tends to rely on expensive processes or proprietary tools, out of reach for smaller clubs and independent researchers. The computer-vision literature for football centres on detection, tracking, and jersey-number reading, almost always inside large, multi-stage pipelines. One narrower problem is left out: classifying the role from a single broadcast crop, with a comparison that is at once systematic, explainable, and attentive to data efficiency. That is the focus here. We classify four roles using 15,636 crops extracted from a public dataset annotated in YOLO format, with 663 match images, and evaluate three approaches: a custom CNN and two transfer-learning models, MobileNetV2 and ResNet50. The original training, validation, and test splits were kept against leakage, with balancing applied only to training. Grad-CAM and SHAP examined the models' decisions; robustness was measured under five corruptions typical of broadcasts, each at five severity levels. The central result is surprising. ResNet50 obtained the highest test accuracy (84.0\%), but concentrated almost everything on the player class, collapsing to a macro F1-score of just 0.23. The custom CNN, with only 0.46 million parameters, was the most balanced (77.9\% accuracy and 0.67 macro F1-score). In short: accuracy alone misleads under class imbalance, and smaller models can outperform more complex architectures once performance, interpretability, and robustness are weighed together.
\end{abstract}

\item A 0.46M-parameter custom CNN is compared against fine-tuned MobileNetV2 and ResNet50.

\item ResNet50 reaches 84\% accuracy but collapses to a single class (0.23 macro F1).
\item Robustness tests under five broadcast corruptions reveal degenerate invariance.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{Application Background and Practical Importance}
Football is one of the most widely followed sports in the world. Each professional match is recorded by multiple broadcast cameras, and the result is hours of video that feed technical, statistical, and commercial analysis.

Coaches, performance analysts, scouts, broadcasters, and refereeing teams all rely on this material to decide. In many of these settings, having objective data about what happened on the pitch is no longer a luxury but a routine part of decision-making.

Almost all of this analysis begins with the same step: identifying what sits in each region of the image. Before measuring performance, generating statistics, or reconstructing game events, one must know whether an object is the ball, a goalkeeper, an outfield player, or a referee.

That step, however, is still largely manual or dependent on expensive commercial solutions. Manual annotation consumes time, varies from annotator to annotator, and does not scale well to large volumes of matches.

The practical effect is twofold. Analyses arrive late or inconsistent, and the burden falls hardest on those with fewer resources, widening the technological gap between large clubs and smaller teams.

Automating the identification of roles in broadcast images attacks exactly this bottleneck. A reliable model would cut the manual effort of annotation and make analysis tools more accessible across different levels of football. Figure~\ref{fig:samples} shows examples of the four roles considered here.

\subsection{Machine Learning and Computer Vision Background}
From a machine-learning point of view, classifying the role of an object in a match is an image-recognition problem. The decision rests on what is visible in the crop: colour, contrast, shape, texture, and the relative position of the object within the scene.

Each class leaves its own cues, though rarely clean ones. Goalkeepers and referees separate from outfield players mostly through kit colour and contrast with the other athletes. The ball is small, roughly circular, and carries texture that shifts with resolution and framing. Outfield players, finally, are the most common class and occupy most crops, which skews both the data distribution and the behaviour of the classifiers.

Classical computer vision would attack this with hand-crafted features: colour histograms, edge, texture, and shape descriptors. They work in controlled scenarios but crumble under the real conditions of a broadcast. Variable lighting, different camera angles, motion blur, video compression, partial occlusions, and look-alike kits change the appearance of objects enough that rules based on fixed features lose generalisation when the match, stadium, or capture condition changes.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) offer a more suitable alternative for this kind of visual variation, because they automatically learn a hierarchy of features directly from the pixels. In the first layers, the network tends to capture simple patterns, such as edges, colours, and local contrasts; in the intermediate layers, it combines these signals into object parts; and in the deeper layers, it represents more complete and discriminative visual structures~\cite{krizhevsky2012imagenet,simonyan2015very}. This ability reduces the dependence on manual feature engineering and explains the broad adoption of CNNs in modern image-classification tasks~\cite{he2016deep,deng2009imagenet}.

In sport this matters because the useful information is not only in individual pixels but in the spatial organisation of the crop. For a player or a referee, the torso concentrates much of the kit-colour evidence, while the relative position of body, legs, and background helps separate look-alike objects. The CNN learns these combinations of shape, colour, and local context that would be hard to specify robustly by hand.

The obstacle is practical. Deep CNNs demand large amounts of labelled data to train from scratch without overfitting, yet public football datasets are small and almost always dominated by the player class. It is this tension between representational capacity, available data, and class balance that justifies the comparative design of this study, in which a custom CNN and transfer-learning models are evaluated under the same protocol.

\subsection{Transfer Learning for the Selected Problem}
Training a deep CNN from scratch is risky when labelled data is scarce. With few samples, the network tends to memorise quirks of the training set instead of learning general patterns, which inflates overfitting and can destabilise training.

Transfer learning eases this. The idea is to start from a network already trained on a large dataset, such as ImageNet, which during that training learned generic visual features --- edges, colours, textures, shapes --- reusable in other vision tasks~\cite{deng2009imagenet}.

Adapting it to the new problem is simple: the final classification layer is removed and replaced by a new one with this study's classes. The rest of the network, the backbone, can stay frozen as a feature extractor or have part of its layers unfrozen for fine-tuning with the football images.

MobileNetV2 enters as the lightweight option. Its depthwise separable convolutions cut parameters and computational cost, which makes it appealing for modest hardware or whenever a small model is wanted~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2,martins2025mobilenet}. ResNet50 represents the opposite end: deeper and higher-capacity, leaning on residual connections that ease the training of deep networks, at the cost of more parameters and a greater risk of overfitting when data is scarce~\cite{he2016deep}.

Placing MobileNetV2, ResNet50, and a custom CNN side by side exposes the balance between capacity, cost, and per-class performance --- and, at bottom, answers whether more parameters help in this problem or whether a smaller architecture is enough. The technical details of each model are left to the Methodology.

\subsection{Explainable AI and Reliability}

High accuracy does not prove that a model learned the right patterns. On imbalanced data the trap is larger: favouring the most common class is enough to look good in aggregate. Here that would mean predicting almost everything as player while ignoring ball, goalkeeper, and referee.

There is also the question of where the model looks. In a reliable application, one expects attention on the object --- the player's body, the referee's kit, the shape of the ball. When the decision leans on the background, the pitch, or signals unrelated to the class, predictions work in specific situations and break in new ones.

To examine this behaviour, we turn to explainable-AI methods. Grad-CAM produces heatmaps pointing to the most influential regions in the classification~\cite{selvaraju2020gradcam,chattopadhay2018gradcampp}; SHAP adds to that picture which parts of the image push the prediction up or down~\cite{lundberg2017unified,aldughayfiq2023retinoblastoma}.

Together, the two techniques say not only whether the model is right but why it is right or wrong. We therefore treat explainability as part of the reliability analysis --- not as a visual ornament at the end of the pipeline.

\subsection{Research Gap}
Computer vision for football has concentrated on object detection, multi-player tracking, re-identification, and jersey-number reading. Almost always these tasks live inside larger pipelines, built on benchmark datasets such as SoccerNet~\cite{giancola2018soccernet,deliege2021soccernetv2,somers2024multitask}. They are important contributions, but they set aside a narrower problem: classifying the role of an object from a single broadcast crop, treated as a task in its own right.

Looking across these studies, a few gaps recur. There is no direct comparison between purpose-built CNNs and transfer-learning models under identical experimental conditions. Class imbalance is mentioned often but rarely handled rigorously --- especially regarding the separation of training, validation, and test, and per-class analysis. The joint use of Grad-CAM and SHAP is still rare, and so are robustness tests under broadcast-typical degradations such as noise, compression, and motion blur. Computational efficiency and deployment cost, in turn, usually take a back seat to the traditional metrics.

It is in this gap that the present work positions itself, bringing together model comparison, explainability, robustness, and efficiency in a single experimental protocol aimed at role classification in football.

\subsection{Problem Definition}
The problem is to automatically classify four roles in football images --- ball, goalkeeper, player, and referee --- from individual crops extracted from television broadcasts. The input is an image with one already-annotated object; the output is that object's class.

The main complication is imbalance. Outfield players dominate the samples, while ball and referee appear far less often. Add to this that, in certain situations, the classes look alike, and the difficulty grows.

The underlying question is how far transfer-learning models actually outperform a custom CNN built specifically for the problem. Beyond accuracy, what matters is the effect of these choices on class balance, efficiency, robustness, and interpretability. In practice, the goal is to find solutions viable in resource-constrained settings --- smaller clubs, independent performance-analysis initiatives.

\subsection{Aim and Objectives}
The aim of this work is to develop and evaluate a system based on convolutional neural networks capable of automatically classifying different roles present in football match images, combining predictive performance, interpretability, and computational efficiency.

The aim unfolds into concrete objectives:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Analyse and pre-process the public dataset: extract the crops from the YOLO annotations and characterise the class imbalance.
    \item Build a low-cost custom CNN to serve as a baseline.
    \item Implement the two transfer-learning models, MobileNetV2 and ResNet50.
    \item Compare the three architectures by accuracy, precision, recall, per-class F1-score, and macro F1-score.
    \item Measure efficiency: number of parameters, model size, and behaviour over training.
    \item Investigate the decisions with Grad-CAM and SHAP.
    \item Test robustness under different image degradations and dissect the main types of error.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Research Questions}

Based on the problem presented, this study is guided by the following research questions:

\begin{itemize}
    \item RQ1: How well can CNN models classify the four roles present in football match images using a public dataset?
    \item RQ2: Which approach offers the best balance for this task: a custom CNN or transfer-learning models?
    \item RQ3: How does class imbalance affect the interpretation of the results, especially when comparing accuracy and macro F1-score?
    \item RQ4: Do the visualisations generated by Grad-CAM and SHAP indicate that the models are using relevant regions of the image to make their decisions?
    \item RQ5: How do the models behave under common degradations in sports broadcasts, such as noise, compression, and blur?
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Contributions and Novelty}
The central contribution is a comparative evaluation of role classification in football that brings together, in a single experimental pipeline, performance, explainability, robustness, and computational efficiency.

In detail, the work offers:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A reproducible pipeline that turns a dataset originally annotated for detection into a four-class classification benchmark.
    \item A controlled comparison between the custom CNN of about 0.46 million parameters and two well-established transfer-learning backbones, MobileNetV2 and ResNet50.
    \item The joint use of Grad-CAM and SHAP to audit decisions and flag inadequate behaviour, such as reliance on shortcuts.
    \item A robustness evaluation under degradations typical of broadcasts.
    \item Evidence of how much imbalance distorts the reading: without macro F1-score and per-class metrics, accuracy alone masks a model's collapse onto the majority class.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Report Organisation}

The remainder of the report runs as follows. Section~\ref{sec:litreview} reviews the work on sports image analysis, CNNs, transfer learning, explainability, and robustness. Section~\ref{sec:methodology} describes the dataset, the preprocessing, the models, and the experimental protocol. Section~\ref{sec:results} brings the results --- classification metrics, per-class analysis, explainability, and robustness. Section~\ref{sec:discussion} interprets all of this, discusses limitations, and points to future directions. Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} closes with the conclusions.

\section{Literature Review}
\label{sec:litreview}

\subsection{Image-Based Machine Learning in the Application Domain}

Image analysis in football has changed in nature over the last few years. Early systems lived on manual rules --- colour, motion, object position. As machine learning advanced, those rules gave way to models that pull visual patterns straight from the data.

The first methods segmented players by background subtraction and colour information, especially the dominant colour of the pitch; kit colour then served to group athletes and separate teams. The strategy paid off in controlled scenarios but was fragile under changes in lighting, angle, shadow, and broadcast quality.

Then came the era of classical methods with handcrafted descriptors. Colour, edge, texture, and shape were extracted from the frames and fed into classifiers such as SVMs or random forests. More flexible than fixed rules, yes, but still hostage to heavy manual effort in choosing and tuning features for each new scenario.

The leap came with deep learning. Large annotated datasets, such as SoccerNet and its later versions, drove models for event spotting, tracking, and match understanding~\cite{giancola2018soccernet,deliege2021soccernetv2}. With more data, it became feasible to train networks that learn richer visual representations and lean less on hand-written rules.

Today, deep models dominate sports video analysis precisely because they absorb variation in lighting, angle, and appearance --- and broadcast images rarely come under a fixed condition. Against manual pipelines, deep networks handle this variability better when given adequate data~\cite{liang2025basketball}.

Not everything was solved. The ball may appear with few pixels and under blur; players get partially occluded; referees blur into other elements of the scene; and the classes do not appear in equal proportions --- outfield players are far more common than ball, goalkeeper, and referee. These are exactly the problems of the task in this work. That is why the review does not stop at the models' average performance: it also looks at imbalance, robustness to degradations, and the reliability of the predictions.

\subsection{CNN-Based Methods for the Selected Task}

CNN-based methods rarely stand alone in the football literature; they come embedded in larger tasks, such as detection and tracking. Role identification --- player, ball, referee --- enters as a cog in the pipeline, not as a classification problem in its own right.

Much of this work uses YOLO-family detectors, or variants, to locate elements on the pitch. They do well on the large, frequent classes, such as players and referees. The ball resists: small, fast, and often blurred, occluded, or low-resolution, it tends to drag down the precision of the whole system~\cite{liang2025basketball,giancola2018soccernet}.

A separate line explores role-aware visual representations. Part-based embeddings, trained jointly for re-identification, team, and role, show that a single backbone can learn cues useful for telling functions apart on the pitch~\cite{somers2024multitask}. Role information, then, is present in the images --- but it is almost always studied inside broader pipelines.

Some limitations recur. Proprietary or very large benchmark datasets make comparison with smaller, accessible scenarios difficult. Heavy backbones and aggregate metrics such as mAP, excellent for detection, hide per-class behaviour --- and on an imbalanced problem a good average can mask failure on the rare classes. Preprocessing varies widely: some only resize, others crop guided by detection or tracking, which blurs how much of the performance is the model and how much is the earlier stages. Few clearly analyse the effect of balancing on ball, goalkeeper, and referee.

A more serious flaw lies in the data split. Spreading crops from the same frame, or from neighbouring frames, across training, validation, and test leaks information: the model ends up evaluated on images nearly identical to those it trained on, and the numbers inflate. To avoid this, we keep the original split at the match level and evaluate each role separately --- which gives a more honest read of performance, especially on imbalance and on the reliability of predictions for less frequent objects.

\subsection{Transfer-Learning Architectures}

Two pre-trained backbones anchor the experimental comparison: MobileNetV2 and ResNet50, chosen because they sit at opposite ends of the spectrum between efficiency and capacity. The former prioritises low cost; the latter, depth and parameter count.

MobileNetV2 was conceived as a lean architecture for vision. Inverted residual blocks, linear bottlenecks, and depthwise separable convolutions cut operations and parameters without giving up good representations. With about three million parameters, it fits scenarios with limited resources or a need for small models~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2,martins2025mobilenet}.

ResNet50 goes the other way. Its residual shortcut connections ease the flow of information between layers and make it feasible to train deep networks capable of more complex representations --- hence its widespread use in image classification. The price is steep: about twenty-five million parameters, more memory, and, in general, more data to generalise well~\cite{he2016deep}.

On small datasets, this contrast between capacity and efficiency becomes decisive. Comparative studies show that lightweight backbones match or beat deeper models when paired with regularisation, augmentation, and learning-rate control, whereas deeper networks overfit more easily under limited training~\cite{martins2025mobilenet}.

Other architectures --- EfficientNet, DenseNet, Inception, Xception --- would also fit, each with its own trade-offs between depth, parameters, cost, and performance~\cite{tan2019efficientnet,huang2017densely,szegedy2016rethinking,chollet2017xception}. We leave them out to keep the comparison focused. Pitting MobileNetV2, ResNet50, and the custom CNN against one another is already enough to test whether more capacity truly buys more performance here --- because, on small and imbalanced data, counting parameters does not guarantee balanced accuracy across the classes.

\subsection{Preprocessing and Data Augmentation}

With little data, preprocessing weighs heavily. Seemingly minor decisions --- the final image size, the form of normalisation, the type of crop --- shape which patterns the network can learn.

The basics are resizing to a fixed resolution, normalising the pixels, and cropping the region of interest. They are also the steps demanded by ImageNet pre-trained backbones, which expect inputs with a format and scale compatible with the original training~\cite{deng2009imagenet}.

Augmentation is the main weapon against sample scarcity and overfitting. Rotation, translation, zoom, brightness variation, and horizontal flipping generate new versions of the training images without extra annotation, helping the model capture more general patterns on small or imbalanced datasets~\cite{lewy2023augmentation}.

There is a catch: augmentation must preserve the label. Some transformations erase or hide the very trait that defines the class. Where orientation, colour, or texture carry information, aggressive augmentation hurts rather than helps.

For football crops, horizontal flipping is safe --- mirroring the image does not change the role, and player, ball, goalkeeper, and referee keep their labels. Strong colour changes, however, are off-limits, because kit colour is one of the few cues that separate goalkeepers and referees from outfield players.

On skewed datasets, balancing sits alongside augmentation. The usual recipes are oversampling, augmentation targeted at minority classes, undersampling of the majority class, and loss reweighting~\cite{ghosh2024imbalance} --- and each affects training differently. There is no silver bullet: the best choice depends on the distribution, the class sizes, the model, and the metric being prioritised, which is exactly why per-class performance and macro F1-score must be looked at, not just accuracy.

Here we opt for label-preserving augmentations, undersampling only of training, and class weighting. The combination curbs the imbalance without touching validation and test, letting the minority classes be analysed under realistic conditions.

\subsection{Model Evaluation and Reliability}

Evaluating image classifiers admits several metrics. The everyday ones are accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC-AUC, and the confusion matrix; in detection and segmentation, mAP, IoU, and the Dice coefficient join in.

Even with so many options, many studies still crown overall accuracy as the main measure. That misleads when the dataset is imbalanced: if one class dominates, favouring it is enough to inflate accuracy, however poor the performance on the rest.

The extreme case is instructive. If most crops are player, always predicting ``player'' gets a lot right overall and zeroes ball, goalkeeper, and referee. Overall accuracy looks acceptable; the per-class metrics expose a model that never learned the task in a balanced way.

Hence the recommendation, on skewed data, to report metrics that light up the rare classes --- macro F1-score, per-class recall, and the full confusion matrix~\cite{ghosh2024imbalance}. The macro F1-score is particularly valuable because it gives equal weight to every class, whatever its size.

There is also the reliability of the results. Calibration, repeated runs, and confidence intervals still receive little attention in applied sports vision, which makes it hard to tell whether a difference between models is stable or hostage to a particular split or run.

Since our dataset is dominated by players, the evaluation puts macro F1-score and per-class behaviour at the centre. Overall accuracy is still reported, but never read on its own --- and we deliberately show the cases where it and the macro F1-score disagree, because that is where reliability is decided in an imbalanced scenario.

\subsection{Explainable AI in Image Analysis}

Explainable-AI methods reveal which parts of the input weigh on a model's decision. In image classification this matters because the right class can come from the wrong cues --- background, shadow, artefacts. Beyond the numbers, then, it pays to check whether the network actually looks at regions tied to the object of interest.

\subsubsection{Grad-CAM}

Grad-CAM produces a localisation map for a specific class, weighting the activations of a convolutional layer by the gradients of the target class with respect to that layer~\cite{selvaraju2020gradcam}. Out of this comes a heatmap that highlights the regions most influential in the prediction.

Its strength is simplicity: it needs only a forward pass and a partial backward pass for the gradients, and it runs on most CNNs without touching the architecture. That is why it spread to medical imaging, industrial inspection, and so many other vision tasks.

Here, what matters is whether the model looks at the right object. For role classification, we expect attention on the player's body, the referee's kit, the goalkeeper's area, or the ball itself. If the map lights up mostly the background, the pitch, or regions unrelated to the object, that is a bad sign.

Grad-CAM is not flawless, though. Born from a deep convolutional layer, it has low spatial resolution and must be upscaled to the original size, which blurs the localisation. Grad-CAM++ was proposed to sharpen this, especially when there are multiple objects or relevant regions~\cite{chattopadhay2018gradcampp}.

\subsubsection{SHAP}

SHAP comes from cooperative game theory. It gives each part of the input a contribution value for the prediction, separating what raises from what lowers the probability of a class~\cite{lundberg2017unified}. The result tells not just where the model looked, but in which direction each region pushed the decision.

In images, the procedure splits the input into regions or superpixels, masks them in different combinations, and watches how the predicted probability swings. From those swings comes a contribution map showing what supports and what weakens the prediction.

Its advantage is stability: SHAP explanations tend to be more consistent than those of some model-agnostic methods, which makes it useful to audit classifiers and compare evidence across predictions~\cite{aldughayfiq2023retinoblastoma,schorr2023interpretability}. In our case it complements Grad-CAM with a finer reading of the regions.

The cost is computational. Estimating the contributions means evaluating the model many times on the same image, under different masks, which limits how many examples can be explained in practice --- all the more with large models or images with many regions.

\subsubsection{Limitations of Explainability}

Useful as they are, these methods do not prove that the model learned correctly. A convincing heatmap helps the analysis but does not guarantee an adequate causal basis for the decision~\cite{nazir2023survey}.

Saliency maps and attribution methods are sensitive to preprocessing, to the chosen layer, to the masking reference, and even to small changes in the input. Two similar images can yield different explanations, even with the same final prediction.

There is also the risk of highlighting regions merely correlated with the label. The pitch or a patch of background may travel with a given class without being the cause of the classification; the explanation then reveals a learned pattern --- possibly fragile outside the test set.

For all this, we use Grad-CAM and SHAP together, comparing their explanations and cross-checking them against correct and incorrect predictions. Neither counts as absolute truth; both are support tools for understanding the classifiers' behaviour.

\subsection{Robustness, Generalisation, and Deployment}

Real broadcast images rarely arrive in ideal conditions. A match brings motion blur, defocus, sensor noise, lighting swings, partial occlusions, and lossy compression --- factors that distort the objects and stall classification, especially when the ball is tiny or a player is partly covered.

The usual way to gauge this is through benchmarks of common corruptions: degradations are applied at controlled severity levels, and the drop in performance is measured against the clean images~\cite{hendrycks2019benchmarking}. One then sees how the model reacts as the input drifts away from the test conditions.

A recurring finding from such evaluations: two models with similar accuracy on clean images can diverge sharply under degradation. One holds up under noise or compression; the other falls apart. Robustness, therefore, cannot be inferred from overall accuracy --- it must be measured on its own.

Real deployment also charges computational costs. For clubs without resources, academic projects, or systems on limited hardware, model size, inference time, and memory matter as much as accuracy. There, compact backbones such as MobileNetV2 can beat larger models even when the gap on clean images is small~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2,martins2025mobilenet}.

We evaluate robustness with five types of corruption at five severity levels, measuring not only the drop in performance but how it converses with what the explanations reveal. The detail is crucial: a model that collapses to a single class can look artificially stable under corruption while never classifying the objects reliably.

\subsection{Literature Review Comparison Matrix}

Table~\ref{tab:literature_matrix} compares studies related to image classification and computer vision applied to sport. The comparison considers the dimensions most important for this work: studied problem, dataset, number of classes, dataset size, preprocessing, models used, use of transfer learning, class balancing, comparison across multiple models, Grad-CAM, SHAP, robustness test, external validation, statistical test, efficiency analysis, main contribution, and main limitation.

The matrix does not aim to rank papers; it exposes recurring methodological patterns --- what is already common practice and what remains neglected in applied sports vision.

The broad picture: transfer learning and multi-model comparison appear often; the joint use of Grad-CAM and SHAP is rare; and robustness tests with controlled corruptions barely show up in this domain.

Other gaps stand out. External validation and formal statistical tests are little used, which weakens any claim about stability. And many works still settle for aggregate metrics, accuracy or mAP, without dissecting per-class performance --- a choice that, on imbalanced football data, hides failures precisely on the minority classes.

Efficiency gets thin attention. Even when model size or inference time appear, they rarely enter the same discussion as the balance between accuracy and per-class performance --- a relationship that is decisive for real applications with scarce resources.

The last row sums up our proposal: balancing only on training, a controlled comparison across three models, dual explainability (Grad-CAM and SHAP), and robustness under five corruptions, all over a leakage-free split, in pursuit of a more realistic and reliable evaluation.

\subsection{Literature Synthesis and Identified Gap}

A few practices recur across the reviewed works: transfer learning, comparison between architectures, and standard detection or classification metrics. The field, then, already has consolidated methods for evaluating vision models on sports images.

The toolset is stable too. YOLO detectors locate objects in sports scenes; ImageNet pre-trained backbones populate the classification tasks. For limited datasets, they make a solid starting point.

Yet questions linger. One of them: do deeper backbones pay off for their cost when data is scarce? Several studies suggest that lighter models generalise just as well, or better, once paired with regularisation, augmentation, and well-controlled training.

The sharpest gaps are in how things are evaluated. Dual explainability is rare, robustness under controlled degradations barely appears, and the reliance on aggregate metrics (accuracy, mAP) keeps hiding failures on skewed data. Leakage-free splits and per-class analysis also get little attention.

We attack these points head-on. The match-level split curbs leakage between training, validation, and test; balancing stays on training, with class weighting; and three models --- custom CNN, MobileNetV2, ResNet50 --- are compared under one protocol. Grad-CAM and SHAP interpret the decisions, and five corruptions gauge robustness.

It is this combination --- performance, class balance, explainability, robustness, and efficiency in a single protocol --- that sets the study apart and organises the methodology of the next section.

\section{Methodology}
\label{sec:methodology}

\subsection{Research Design}

The study is experimental and quantitative. The task is single-label: each crop receives exactly one of four mutually exclusive classes --- ball, goalkeeper, player, or referee.

The design is comparative. A custom CNN, trained from scratch, competes with two transfer-learning models, MobileNetV2 and ResNet50, all under the same data, the same preprocessing, and the same training controls --- the condition for a fair comparison.

Explainability is no appendix; it is a central part of the evaluation. Grad-CAM and SHAP show which regions drive the decisions, while per-class metrics, confusion matrices, and robustness tests with corrupted images take care of reliability.

The train/validation/test split follows the dataset's original structure, which reduces leakage between partitions when crops look alike. The test set stays sealed, used only in the final evaluation.

Figure~\ref{fig:workflow} summarises the complete flow of the study, from data preparation to model evaluation.

\subsection{Dataset Description}

\subsubsection{Dataset Origin and Accessibility}

The dataset is \textit{Football Players Detection}, from Roboflow Universe, under a CC BY 4.0 licence~\cite{roboflow2024football}. It holds real broadcast images annotated with the four roles of interest: ball, goalkeeper, player, and referee.

We downloaded the data through the Roboflow Python API, in YOLO format, with access in 2026. The format delivers, per image, the bounding boxes and the object labels --- exactly what allows extracting the crops for classification.

The choice rested on three reasons. The dataset carries real match frames, which brings the study closer to a practical scenario; its annotations already cover the four classes; and it is free to reuse, with an original split between training, validation, and test.

Keeping that split matters for containing leakage between partitions. And the dataset's modest size, far from a defect, brings the problem closer to settings with little labelled data --- academic projects, smaller clubs, independent performance-analysis initiatives.

\subsubsection{Dataset Composition}

The dataset has 663 annotated images, split by the authors into 612 for training, 38 for validation, and 13 for test. Each image is JPEG, annotated in the YOLO standard, with one bounding box per object in one of the four classes.

To convert detection into classification, every bounding box was cropped independently, so each annotated object became an individual sample. The process yielded 15,636 crops in total.

Crop resolution varies a great deal, since objects sit at different positions and distances from the camera. The ball may occupy a handful of pixels when far away or in motion; a player near the camera produces a much larger crop. That spread raises the difficulty and, again, mirrors the real conditions of a broadcast.

Data preparation turned up no corrupted or unreadable files. The YOLO annotations served directly as the source of labels, preserving the link between each bounding box and its original class.

Table~\ref{tab:dataset} lays out the full composition --- crops per class in each partition and the effect of the balancing applied only to training. The raw dataset has 15,636 crops, overwhelmingly player: 13,239 of them.

\subsubsection{Class Definition}

The four classes cover the main roles visible in the broadcast. The ball is the smallest object: near-circular, with its own texture and strong contrast against the pitch. The goalkeeper, who defends the goal, wears a kit deliberately distinct from outfield players and referees --- a strong cue for classification. The outfield-player class gathers the athletes of both teams who are not goalkeepers; it is the most frequent class and accounts for most of the annotated objects.

Referees are the officials on the pitch, usually in a neutral or dark kit, different from the two teams. In distant or low-resolution images, however, their appearance can blur into that of goalkeepers or players.

\subsubsection{Dataset Quality Assessment}

The dataset's chief limitation is the heavy class imbalance. Outfield players exceed 13 thousand crops while ball, goalkeeper, and referee appear far less often --- fertile ground for the model to favour the majority class during training.

Visual quality is a second concern. Many ball crops, and some distant players, come at very low resolution; at times the object spans only a few pixels, hard to classify even for a human eye.

Some crops also carry partial occlusion or a wide margin of background around the object, a side effect of the axis-aligned rectangular bounding boxes: stretches of pitch, other players, or nearby elements end up inside the crop.

Crops from the same frame, finally, tend to be nearly identical. Spreading them across training, validation, and test would leak information, evaluating the model on images all but copied from training. That is why we kept the original split exactly as provided, at the image and match level. Removing cross-partition duplicates was unnecessary --- the original separation already keeps crops from the same visual context from mixing.

\subsubsection{Dataset Visualisation}

Figure~\ref{fig:samples} shows representative examples of the four classes. The crops make the differences between ball, goalkeeper, player, and referee visible --- but also how close some classes sit: goalkeepers, referees, and outfield players share similar body shapes, separated mainly by colour, contrast, and local context.

Figure~\ref{fig:distribution} shows the class distribution in the training set after balancing. In this process, the ball, goalkeeper, and referee classes keep all of their available crops, since they are already below the limit, while only the player class is capped to reduce its dominance. This step seeks to make training less biased towards player, without changing the validation and test sets.

Together, the two figures make the main challenges of the dataset clearer. The first highlights the visual similarity between some classes, while the second shows the effect of the imbalance and of the strategy used to reduce it in training. For this reason, these visualisations also help to justify the later analyses of balancing, per-class performance, and explainability.

\subsection{Data Preparation}

\subsubsection{Data Cleaning}

Preparation began by reading the YOLO annotations. For each image, every bounding box was taken from its label file, and the normalised coordinates were converted to absolute pixels so the object could be cropped straight from the original image.

Each box became an individual crop. Boxes yielding empty, invalid, or zero-area regions were discarded as useless for training. The rest were saved to disk, organised by original partition and class.

No manual label correction was done: the annotations shipped with the dataset stand as ground truth here. The process turned up no unreadable or corrupted image file.

\subsubsection{Data Splitting}

The original split held throughout the study. The dataset already separates at the match and image level --- 612 images for training, 38 for validation, 13 for test --- and each crop inherited the partition of its source image.

After extraction, the full set reached 15,636 crops. The test partition, 307 crops, was sealed for the final evaluation: no training, no hyperparameter tuning, no model selection touched it.

Keeping the separation at the image level guards against leakage. Since many crops share a frame, mixing them across partitions would evaluate the model on examples nearly identical to those it trained on. So we performed no new random split and no shuffling between partitions --- the dataset's structure stays intact, and the evaluation stays realistic.

\subsubsection{Image Preprocessing}

All crops were converted to RGB and resized to 224$\times$224 pixels, the input expected by the ImageNet pre-trained backbones, MobileNetV2 and ResNet50 included~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2,he2016deep}. Pixel intensities went from integers to floating point in $[0,1]$ by dividing by 255, which shrinks the numerical scale and keeps processing identical across models. Resizing used bilinear interpolation, with no aggressive cropping, contrast equalisation, or strong colour changes --- operations that could erase cues the task depends on, kit colour above all, the main signal separating goalkeepers, referees, and outfield players.

The same preprocessing ran for all three models, so that any difference in the results traces back to the architectures and the training, not to the image preparation.

\subsubsection{Data Augmentation}

Augmentation ran only on the training set, at run time. Validation and test stayed untouched, so the evaluation reflects performance on unmodified images.

The transformations all preserve the label: rotation up to 20 degrees, horizontal and vertical shifts up to 15\%, zoom up to 15\%, brightness between 80\% and 120\%, and horizontal flipping. Each adds visual variety without changing the object's class. Rotation, shift, and zoom mimic small variations in framing, distance, and position within the crop; brightness stands in for the lighting differences of stadiums and broadcasts; and horizontal flipping fits because mirroring leaves the role intact --- ball, goalkeeper, player, and referee keep their labels.

We avoided extreme colour distortions on purpose. Kit colour is a key cue for telling goalkeepers and referees from outfield players, and strong colour changes would strip away one of the most relevant pieces of evidence --- against good augmentation practice whenever colour carries meaning for the label~\cite{lewy2023augmentation}.

\subsubsection{Handling Class Imbalance}

Two complementary strategies handled the imbalance. The first was random undersampling of the training set, capping each class at 1,500 crops --- which curbed the dominance of the player class while keeping every available crop of ball, goalkeeper, and referee. The second was class weights during training, set inversely proportional to each class's frequency, so that errors on the rarer classes weigh more on the loss and the model is pushed away from betting everything on the majority.

Undersampling touched only training. Validation and test kept their natural distribution, with no artificial balancing --- a deliberate choice, since it evaluates the models under conditions closer to deployment, where classes also appear at uneven rates~\cite{ghosh2024imbalance}. The aim is to curb the player-class bias during training without distorting the final evaluation, which is exactly why macro F1-score, per-class recall, and the confusion matrix become essential to tell whether balancing genuinely helps the minority classes.

\subsection{Model Development}

\subsubsection{Baseline: Custom CNN}

The first architecture is a custom CNN trained from scratch. It takes 224$\times$224$\times$3 inputs and was designed as a compact baseline for the role-classification task.

Its core is four convolutional blocks, with 32, 64, 128, and 256 filters. Each block runs a 3$\times$3 convolution with padding, then ReLU, batch normalisation, 2$\times$2 max pooling, and 25\% dropout; block by block, the spatial resolution shrinks while the feature maps deepen~\cite{ioffe2015batch,srivastava2014dropout}. After the convolutional stack, global average pooling condenses the maps into a compact representation, followed by a dense layer of 256 units with ReLU, batch normalisation, and 50\% dropout. The output layer has four softmax units, one per class.

Keeping it compact was a deliberate choice: with 458,180 trainable parameters, it lets us test whether a small model trained directly on the problem's data can stand up to larger pre-trained backbones. Table~\ref{tab:hyperparams} summarises the configuration, and Figure~\ref{fig:architecture} shows the diagram.

\subsubsection{Transfer Model One: MobileNetV2}

The first transfer-learning model builds on MobileNetV2 pre-trained on ImageNet. We dropped the original classification head and kept only the convolutional backbone as a feature extractor~\cite{sandler2018mobilenetv2,deng2009imagenet}. On top of it sits a new head for the four classes: global average pooling, a dense layer of 512 units with ReLU, 40\% dropout, a second dense layer of 256 units with ReLU, 30\% dropout, and a final softmax with four units.

Training ran in two phases. First, the whole backbone stayed frozen and only the new head trained --- enough to point the output at the four roles without yet disturbing the ImageNet representations. Then the last 30 layers of the backbone were unfrozen and trained alongside the head, at a lower learning rate, to nudge the high-level features toward the football domain without wrecking the pre-trained weights. The final model holds about 3.05 million parameters.

\subsubsection{Transfer Model Two: ResNet50}

The second transfer model rests on ResNet50 pre-trained on ImageNet. As with MobileNetV2, the original head gave way to the same custom one --- dense layers, dropout, and a four-class softmax~\cite{he2016deep}. Training again split into two phases: the frozen backbone with only the head trained, then the last 15 layers unfrozen for fine-tuning at a lower learning rate. Unfreezing fewer layers than MobileNetV2 respects the deeper residual structure and limits how many weights shift during the move to the football domain.

The final model has about 24.8 million parameters, more than 50 times the size of the custom CNN. Its inclusion makes it possible to evaluate whether this additional capacity improves classification or whether it increases the risk of overfitting on a small and imbalanced dataset.

\subsubsection{Feature-Extraction and Fine-Tuning Strategy}

Both transfer models followed the same script: freeze the pre-trained backbone and train only the new head, then unfreeze a final slice of the backbone for fine-tuning alongside the head.

The first step is pure feature extraction. With the head starting from random weights, freezing the backbone steadies the early training and keeps the large initial gradients from abruptly rewriting the ImageNet representations.

The second step unfreezes only the final layers, concentrating adaptation on the task-specific features --- combinations of shape, texture, and colour tied to the football roles --- while the first layers, which capture edges, contrasts, and simple patterns, stay put.

The depth of unfreezing differs by model: 30 layers for MobileNetV2, 15 for ResNet50. Both values allow some adaptation to the football domain without inflating the risk of overfitting on a small, imbalanced dataset.

\subsection{Training Procedure}

\subsubsection{Loss Function}

All models were trained with categorical cross-entropy, the standard loss for multi-class problems with mutually exclusive classes --- and each crop here belongs to exactly one of the four, which makes it a natural fit.

Its weighted form, for a single example, appears in Equation~\eqref{eq:loss}:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L} = -\sum_{c=1}^{C} w_c\, y_c \log(\hat{y}_c),
\label{eq:loss}
\end{equation}
Here $C=4$ is the number of roles, $y_c$ the one-hot ground truth for class $c$, $\hat{y}_c$ the predicted probability for that class, and $w_c$ its weight.

The weights offset the residual imbalance in the training set: rarer classes get larger weights, so their errors weigh more on the total loss. Missing a ball or goalkeeper crop, in other words, costs the model more than missing a player crop.

\subsubsection{Optimiser and Learning Rate}

Every model used the Adam optimiser, chosen for its stable convergence across many deep-learning problems and for needing less manual learning-rate tuning than simpler methods~\cite{kingma2015adam}.

The initial rate was $1\times10^{-3}$ for training the head. In the transfer models, fine-tuning dropped it to $1\times10^{-5}$ (Table~\ref{tab:hyperparams}) to shield the pre-trained weights from large swings in the ImageNet representations. On top of this ran a \textit{ReduceLROnPlateau} schedule, which lowers the rate whenever the validation loss stalls for a set number of epochs, letting training carry on in smaller steps as it nears a stable region.

We applied no explicit weight decay; regularisation came mainly from the dropout and batch normalisation already built into the architectures.

\subsubsection{Training Controls}

Training ran in batches of 32 images, capped at 50 epochs per phase. \textit{EarlyStopping} watched the validation accuracy with a patience of 8 epochs, to cut needless training and curb overfitting, while \textit{ModelCheckpoint} saved the weights with the best validation performance. The results reported here, then, do not come from the last epoch but from the best checkpoint found during training.

Where possible, the random seed was fixed for reproducibility. Since neural-network training still carries sources of variation, best-checkpoint selection remained the main control across all models.

\subsubsection{Hyperparameter Selection}

We ran no exhaustive hyperparameter search. The configurations started from common practice in transfer-learning studies and were tuned only lightly, given the dataset size and the resources of a single GPU~\cite{martins2025mobilenet}. The point was to keep the focus on comparing architectures, not on squeezing the last drop out of each model. Table~\ref{tab:hyperparams} lists the full configuration.

\subsection{Evaluation Framework}

\subsubsection{Primary Predictive Metrics}

Performance was measured with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, always read against the four roles --- ball, goalkeeper, player, and referee. The analysis thus weighs not only the total number of correct predictions but how each class fared.

For a specific role $c$, a true positive (TP) occurs when a crop of class $c$ is correctly predicted as $c$. A false positive (FP) occurs when a crop of another role is predicted as $c$. A false negative (FN) occurs when a crop of class $c$ is predicted as another role.

Accuracy measures the fraction of test crops whose predicted role equals the annotated label. This metric summarises the overall performance of the model, as shown in Equation~\eqref{eq:acc}.
\begin{equation}
\text{Accuracy} = \frac{\text{correctly classified crops}}{\text{total crops}}.
\label{eq:acc}
\end{equation}
Precision and recall were computed separately for each class. Precision indicates, among all the crops predicted as a class, how many actually belong to that class. For example, the precision of the goalkeeper class shows how many crops predicted as goalkeeper were in fact goalkeepers. Recall indicates, among all the real crops of that class, how many were found by the model. Thus, goalkeeper recall shows how many real goalkeepers were correctly classified. These definitions are presented in Equation~\eqref{eq:pr}.
\begin{equation}
\text{Precision}_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FP_c}, \qquad
\text{Recall}_c = \frac{TP_c}{TP_c + FN_c},
\label{eq:pr}
\end{equation}
The F1-score combines precision and recall into a single measure, using the harmonic mean between the two. This metric is useful when it is necessary to consider, at the same time, false positives and false negatives. The F1-score was computed per class, and the macro F1-score was obtained by the simple average of the four roles, as shown in Equation~\eqref{eq:f1}.
\begin{equation}
\text{F1}_c = \frac{2\,\text{Precision}_c\,\text{Recall}_c}{\text{Precision}_c + \text{Recall}_c}, \qquad
\text{macro F1} = \frac{1}{C}\sum_{c=1}^{C}\text{F1}_c.
\label{eq:f1}
\end{equation}
The macro F1-score is our main comparison metric, precisely because it weighs every class equally, whatever its size. On imbalanced data that matters: failures on rare classes such as ball and goalkeeper would otherwise vanish behind the overall accuracy.

\subsubsection{Class-Level Evaluation}

For every model we computed the full confusion matrix on validation and test, plus precision, recall, and F1-score for each of the four classes.

The dataset is dominated by players, and that is exactly why this matters: a model can score high accuracy while ignoring ball, goalkeeper, and referee. The class-level view tells whether the performance is spread evenly or piled onto the majority class.

\subsubsection{Training Behaviour}

Throughout training we logged the accuracy and loss curves for training and validation, using them to read convergence, stability, and any signs of overfitting. We also recorded the epoch of best validation performance and the point where early stopping fired --- because when the training curve keeps climbing while validation flattens or worsens, the model is likely overfitting.

\subsubsection{Computational Efficiency}

Efficiency came down to two measures: the number of trainable parameters and the model size on disk in megabytes. Together they let us compare not just predictive performance but the practical cost of each architecture --- a cost that bears directly on memory use and on whether the model can run on simpler hardware. Since this study targets resource-constrained scenarios, efficiency sits in the analysis alongside accuracy, macro F1-score, and per-class performance.

\subsubsection{Statistical Reliability}

Given the cost of training each model on a single GPU, the results come from the best checkpoint of a single run per architecture; we did not repeat runs to estimate variance or confidence intervals.

Small gaps between models, therefore, are read with caution. Close numbers may sit within the noise of an individual run and are not treated as evidence of statistical significance --- the discussion leans instead on consistent differences in macro F1-score, per-class behaviour, robustness, and explainability. Repeated runs with different seeds and confidence intervals are left for future work.

\subsection{Explainable-AI Methodology}

\subsubsection{Grad-CAM Procedure}

Grad-CAM maps came from the last convolutional layer of each model, taken against the class the classifier itself predicted~\cite{selvaraju2020gradcam} --- which shows the regions that weighed most on the final decision.

The procedure averages the gradients of the class score with respect to the activation maps, uses these as per-channel importance weights, combines them with the activations of the chosen layer, applies ReLU, normalises to $[0,1]$, upscales to the crop size, and overlays the result on the image.

We picked example crops spanning correct and incorrect predictions across the four roles, so we could see whether the models fix attention on the right object or drift to less relevant regions --- the pitch, the background, nearby elements.

\subsubsection{SHAP Procedure}

For SHAP we used the \textit{Partition Explainer}, a model-agnostic method, with an image masker based on \textit{inpainting}. Relying only on forward passes, it stays independent of the architecture's internals and of framework version changes~\cite{lundberg2017unified}.

We explained two test crops per class, estimating the attribution map of the predicted class with 600 masking evaluations each. The result separates positive regions, which raise the probability of the predicted class, from negative ones, which lower it.

We read the positive regions as evidence the model used in favour of the prediction, and the negative regions as parts that pulled against it. This complements Grad-CAM: it shows not just where the model looked but how each region tipped the decision.

\subsubsection{Evaluation of the Explanations}

The explanations were judged qualitatively, on one main criterion: did the attention or attribution land on the target object --- the player's torso, the referee's kit, the goalkeeper, the ball --- or did it scatter onto background regions such as the pitch, the stands, or areas unrelated to the class?

When Grad-CAM and SHAP agree on the same regions, the case that the model uses relevant cues grows stronger. Systematic differences between correct and incorrect predictions, in turn, expose failure patterns --- attention shifted to the background, overuse of context.

A model that keeps high performance yet consistently ignores the object in its explanations is read as possibly leaning on shortcuts. This follows the literature's caution against treating explanation maps as absolute proof of correct reasoning~\cite{nazir2023survey}.

\subsection{Robustness Analysis}

For robustness we corrupted the held-out test crops with five degradations common in broadcasts --- Gaussian blur, additive Gaussian noise, reduced brightness, central occlusion, and JPEG compression --- each at five severity levels plus level zero, the clean image~\cite{hendrycks2019benchmarking}. For every combination of corruption and severity, the whole test set was transformed, reclassified, and scored with accuracy and macro F1-score per model. This reveals how fast performance decays as quality drops, and it also flags pathological behaviour: a model that seems barely affected because it already ignores the visual content and always predicts the same class.

\subsection{Software, Hardware, and Reproducibility}

The experiments were implemented in Python, with TensorFlow and Keras for building, training, and evaluating the models~\cite{tensorflow2015}. Training ran on a workstation with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 GPU.

SHAP explanations came from the SHAP library; the image corruptions from OpenCV and NumPy; the metrics from scikit-learn. The pipeline was split into separate scripts for dataset preparation, balancing, training, Grad-CAM, SHAP, robustness, and inference.

Trained models, figures, and intermediate files were written to a dedicated outputs directory. A reproducible notebook on Kaggle accompanies the study, and the source code is to be released in a public repository --- enough to re-run the whole experiment from the same data and parameters.

\subsection{Ethical and Practical Considerations}

The dataset shows people in a public sports context, under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Even so, broadcast images can raise privacy and consent issues once used beyond role classification --- above all in tasks tied to identifying individuals.

The imbalance carries its own caveat. With some roles barely represented, the system is not equally reliable across classes, and any later use should expect more frequent errors on the minorities: ball, goalkeeper, referee.

The system also confuses visually similar roles, especially in distant, blurred, or low-resolution images. Its predictions, then, should support human judgement rather than replace it --- all the more so in refereeing or other high-impact decisions. In short, the framework is a decision-support tool, not an autonomous referee.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Dataset and Preprocessing Results}

Extracting the YOLO annotations from the 663 images yielded 15,636 usable crops. Preprocessing found no corrupted or unreadable file, and the original labels were kept as provided.

The raw distribution was heavily skewed. Players led with 13,239 crops; the ball trailed far behind at 405; the other classes fell between these extremes (Table~\ref{tab:dataset}). Balancing, applied only to training, capped the player class at 1,500 crops, while ball, goalkeeper, and referee kept every available crop, already below that limit. Figure~\ref{fig:distribution} shows the result.

The original match-level split held throughout. The held-out test set has 307 crops, 258 of them players --- a distribution preserved so the final evaluation mirrors the dataset's real composition. Figure~\ref{fig:samples} gives examples of the four classes, exposing both the visual closeness of goalkeepers, referees, and outfield players and the small size of the ball against everything else.

Together these numbers describe the data behind the experiments and set up the answers to RQ1 and RQ3, on model performance and the effect of class imbalance.

\subsection{Training and Convergence Results}

Figures~\ref{fig:curves_cnn}, \ref{fig:curves_mobile}, and \ref{fig:curves_resnet} show the accuracy and loss curves on training and validation for the three models, each up to early stopping or the best saved checkpoint.

The custom CNN converged gradually. Training and validation curves moved together, with no wide gap, and the validation loss tracked the drop seen in training, varying only slightly from epoch to epoch.

MobileNetV2 converged fast in the first phase, with only the head trainable. Fine-tuning improved the training metrics further, though the validation curve oscillated; the best checkpoint was taken from the peak validation performance.

ResNet50 hit high validation accuracy within the first epochs and barely moved afterwards. The curve looks stable --- but, as the next subsections reveal, that stability hides a degenerate behaviour.

In every model, early stopping fired when the validation accuracy stopped improving, and the reported results use the best checkpoint, not necessarily the last epoch.

\subsection{Overall Model Performance}

Table~\ref{tab:results} compares the three models on the held-out test set --- accuracy, macro precision, macro recall, macro F1-score, weighted F1-score, parameters, and disk size.

By accuracy, ResNet50 led with 84.0\%, ahead of the custom CNN at 77.9\% and MobileNetV2 at 69.1\%. Validation accuracy keeps the same order: 84.4\%, 71.9\%, and 67.1\%.

By macro F1-score the ranking flips. The custom CNN comes first at 0.67, MobileNetV2 follows at 0.60, and ResNet50 falls to the bottom at 0.23.

That is the heart of the comparison: the model with the highest raw accuracy is also the one with the lowest macro F1-score. Figure~\ref{fig:comparison} plots the accuracy side by side --- and answers RQ2, with clear differences between the custom CNN and the transfer-learning models.

\subsection{Class-Level Performance}

Table~\ref{tab:perclass} breaks the F1-score down by class on the held-out test set, where the four classes carry very different weights: 9 ball crops, 11 goalkeeper, 258 player, and 29 referee.

The custom CNN scored 0.94 on ball, 0.30 on goalkeeper, 0.87 on player, and 0.58 on referee --- goalkeeper its weakest point. MobileNetV2 followed the same shape (0.82, 0.18, 0.80, 0.59), again stumbling on goalkeeper.

ResNet50 tells a different story: 0.91 on player and 0.00 on ball, goalkeeper, and referee alike. The confusion matrix is unambiguous --- it labelled every test crop ``player''. And since players make up 258 of 307 crops, roughly 84\%, that single guess buys 84.0\% accuracy. Figures~\ref{fig:cm_cnn}, \ref{fig:cm_mobile}, and \ref{fig:cm_resnet} show the three confusion matrices.

This answers RQ3: the classes behave very differently, and among the models that told more than one role apart, goalkeeper was always the hardest.

\subsection{Explainable-AI Results}

\subsubsection{Grad-CAM Results}

Figures~\ref{fig:gradcam_cnn}, \ref{fig:gradcam_mobile}, and \ref{fig:gradcam_resnet} show the Grad-CAM heatmaps for representative crops, correct predictions in green, errors in red.

For the custom CNN, the heat sits on the main object: the body in player crops, the small rounded region in ball crops. MobileNetV2 behaves much the same on its correct predictions, focusing on the object in many samples, ball and player above all.

ResNet50 breaks the pattern. Its maps are diffuse, loosely attached to the object; in several crops the activation bleeds over the background or nearby areas, with no clear concentration on the predicted class.

\subsubsection{SHAP Results}

Figures~\ref{fig:shap_cnn}, \ref{fig:shap_mobile}, and \ref{fig:shap_resnet} give the SHAP attributions for two test crops per class --- positive regions supporting the predicted class, negative ones pulling against it.

For the custom CNN, the positive evidence lands on the object itself: the torso and body in player crops, the ball region or its immediate surroundings in ball crops. MobileNetV2 again echoes this, with positive attributions on the object in many samples, mostly ball and player, where the support hugs the main shape of the predicted class.

ResNet50, once more, is the outlier. Its positive attributions are weaker and more scattered, in places spread over the background or over regions with no clear tie to the object.

\subsubsection{Comparison of the Explanations}

Grad-CAM and SHAP agree for the custom CNN and MobileNetV2: both methods light up the main object --- the player's body, the region of the ball. For ResNet50 they agree too, but in the opposite direction: both produce explanations that drift off the object and onto the background or nearby regions.

This convergence between the two methods, set beside the per-class results, answers RQ4. The explanations draw a clear visual line between the models with the best macro F1-score and the one with the highest raw accuracy.

\subsection{Robustness Results}

Figure~\ref{fig:robustness} traces the test accuracy of the three models under five corruptions, each at five severity levels, with the clean level as the undegraded baseline.

The custom CNN held up reasonably under mild blur and occlusion, but reduced brightness broke it: accuracy fell from 77.9\% on clean images to about 9\% at the harshest level. Additive Gaussian noise also ate into its performance at higher severities. MobileNetV2 proved sturdier under some blur and JPEG compression --- at moderate severities its accuracy even brushed or slightly topped the clean value --- yet it dropped sharply under intense noise, heavy darkening, and severe central occlusion.

ResNet50 sat at a flat 84.0\% accuracy and 0.23 macro F1-score across every corruption and severity. The invariance is not strength but symptom: predicting ``player'' for every crop, it ignores the image entirely, clean or corrupted alike.

This answers RQ5, mapping how each model reacts when broadcast-typical degradations hit the test images.

\centering

\caption{Test accuracy under five typical broadcast corruptions (blur, additive noise, reduced brightness, central occlusion, and JPEG compression) at five severity levels, with severity zero denoting the clean image. The custom CNN and MobileNetV2 respond to the corruptions as expected, whereas ResNet50 produces a perfectly flat curve because it predicts the majority class for every input, demonstrating that its apparent invariance is a degenerate artefact and not genuine robustness.}
\label{fig:robustness}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Efficiency and Deployment Results}

The efficiency columns of Table~\ref{tab:results} give the parameters and disk size of each model: 0.46 million and 5.4 MB for the custom CNN, 3.05 million and 30 MB for MobileNetV2, 24.8 million and 147 MB for ResNet50. The gap between the custom CNN and ResNet50 is over fiftyfold in parameters --- and yet the smallest model posted the highest macro F1-score on test, 0.67.

This matters for RQ5: the lightest model was also the most balanced across classes. On modest hardware, model size and storage cost weigh directly on whether deployment is even feasible. Figure~\ref{fig:inference} shows a qualitative example on a full frame, with annotated boxes over the detected objects.

\subsection{Comparison with Published Studies}

Any comparison with published studies demands caution. Much of the football literature reports detection metrics such as mAP, on different datasets and splits, whereas we evaluate the classification of already-extracted crops over four classes, with accuracy and macro F1-score. The numbers, then, are not directly comparable to detection, tracking, or game-understanding work~\cite{giancola2018soccernet,deliege2021soccernetv2,somers2024multitask}.

Some patterns still line up qualitatively. In detection, the ball is among the hardest classes --- small, fast, often blurred. Here, with the ball already located and judged as a crop, it lands among the best F1-scores for the custom CNN and MobileNetV2. The contrast is telling: locating the ball in a full frame is one problem; classifying it once cropped is quite another.

Goalkeeper, by contrast, scored lowest among the models that told classes apart --- echoing the difficulties reported in role-aware work, where players, goalkeepers, and referees blur together under certain visual conditions~\cite{somers2024multitask}. And the fact that a compact architecture beats a deeper backbone on macro F1-score matches transfer-learning comparisons in other domains, where lightweight models rival or surpass larger ones on small datasets with adequate regularisation and augmentation~\cite{martins2025mobilenet}.

So the comparison stays qualitative. Differences in dataset, split, task, and protocol forbid any claim of direct superiority over prior work. Even so, the results follow patterns already documented and help place this study within computer vision for sport.
