\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Interpretation of the Dataset and Preprocessing Findings}

The dataset's hardest obstacle turns out to be not the visual difficulty of the images but the sheer imbalance between classes. Players dominate while ball, goalkeeper, and referee appear in far smaller numbers --- which strikes at RQ1, since overall accuracy can look high even when the model never learned all the roles in a balanced way.

Label-preserving augmentation steadied training, the custom CNN most of all: its validation curve hugged the training curve, with a small gap between them. The reading is that moderate transformations --- rotation, shift, zoom, limited brightness, horizontal flipping --- added visual variety without distorting the meaning of the classes.

Balancing only the training set was equally consequential. It loosened the grip of the player class during learning and let the models see more ball, goalkeeper, and referee, while validation and test kept the dataset's natural distribution and so escaped an artificially balanced evaluation. That choice brings the evaluation closer to real deployment, where outfield players genuinely outnumber the ball, goalkeepers, and referees, and where we want to see the models under realistic odds.

Preprocessing preserved the cues that matter. Avoiding aggressive colour changes was the right call, because kit colour is one of the few signals separating goalkeepers, referees, and outfield players --- strong colour shifts would have stripped away exactly that evidence.

For all these precautions, some problems persist. Tiny ball crops, distant players, and the resemblance among goalkeepers, referees, and players keep surfacing in the errors. They belong to the visual nature of the dataset and are not undone by resizing or augmentation. All of this aligns with the literature on imbalance and augmentation, which stresses applying balancing carefully, preserving a realistic evaluation distribution, and keeping augmentations label-valid when colour, orientation, or texture carry meaning for the class~\cite{ghosh2024imbalance,lewy2023augmentation}.

\subsection{Comparative Performance of the CNN Models}

RQ2 makes one thing plain: models cannot be ranked by accuracy alone. Read Table~\ref{tab:results} naively and ResNet50 wins, with the highest test accuracy. The macro F1-score and the per-class view tell the opposite story.

ResNet50 reached 84.0\% by predicting ``player'' for every crop --- and since 258 of the 307 test crops are players, that alone sufficed for high accuracy. The same model scored zero F1 on ball, goalkeeper, and referee, dragging its macro F1-score down to 0.23.

This is a textbook failure mode under imbalance. A high-capacity model, trained on little data with sharp class asymmetry, can settle into a solution driven by the majority frequency: it never learns to separate the roles, it exploits the distribution. Accuracy rewards the trick; macro F1-score punishes it~\cite{ghosh2024imbalance}.

The custom CNN took the best macro F1-score despite being the smallest model. The likely reason is that its tighter capacity, together with the training balancing and class weighting, made the majority-only shortcut less profitable --- so it actually separated the roles, ball and player above all. MobileNetV2 landed in between: its pre-trained backbone supplied useful features, yet the imbalance still pressed on it, leaving a macro F1-score below the custom CNN's but above ResNet50's, with some discriminative power intact.

Fine-tuning, it seems, paid off more for MobileNetV2 than for ResNet50, in line with studies where lightweight backbones adapt better to small datasets under regularisation, augmentation, and learning-rate control~\cite{martins2025mobilenet,sandler2018mobilenetv2}. ResNet50's extra capacity simply did not convert into balance across classes.

The practical lesson of RQ2 is blunt: higher accuracy is not a better model. Selection here should follow the macro F1-score and the per-class behaviour, because those are what reveal whether a classifier learned the four roles or merely cashed in on the most frequent one.

\subsection{Per-Class Reliability and Error Patterns}

RQ3 shows that the models do not fail uniformly across classes. The per-class view exposes which roles are easy to separate and which stay unstable, even after balancing and class weighting.

The ball was the strongest class in the two models that genuinely told roles apart --- 0.94 F1 for the custom CNN, 0.82 for MobileNetV2. Once located and cropped, its near-circular shape, compact size, and contrast with the pitch hand the classifier strong cues.

The goalkeeper sat at the other extreme, the weakest class for both (0.30 and 0.18). The reason fits the class: a goalkeeper's body shape resembles an outfield player's, and the dataset offers far fewer examples, so the model must learn the difference from kit, colour, and context with little to learn from. The referee fell in between --- its usually neutral or dark kit helps separate it from outfield players, but in distant or low-resolution crops, where the colour does not read clearly, it drifts toward goalkeepers or players.

The error types differ sharply. In the custom CNN and MobileNetV2, mistakes mostly mean confusion among the three human roles --- goalkeeper, player, referee. ResNet50 fails differently: it does not confuse specific classes, it predicts ``player'' everywhere, scoring complete error on ball, goalkeeper, and referee.

These errors cost differently in practice. Missing the ball compromises downstream tracking and event analysis; mistaking a goalkeeper for a player distorts positioning, area-occupation, and tactical reads; mistaking a referee for a player corrupts any pipeline that separates participants from officials. The root cause seems to be the same combination throughout --- few examples and high visual similarity between roles --- a pattern also seen in role-aware work, where players, goalkeepers, and other agents stay hard to tell apart under certain conditions~\cite{somers2024multitask}.

The confusion matrices in Figures~\ref{fig:cm_cnn}--\ref{fig:cm_resnet} lay these patterns bare. The implication is concrete: more and more varied goalkeeper crops would likely be the single highest-impact way to lift per-class reliability.

\subsection{Interpretation of Grad-CAM and SHAP}

RQ4 carries some of the study's most important findings, because it shows that numbers need to be paired with visual evidence of behaviour. The question is not only whether the classifier is right but whether it reaches the prediction through regions that make sense.

For the custom CNN and MobileNetV2, Grad-CAM and SHAP say many predictions follow the object itself: the body and kit in player crops, the small rounded area in ball crops. That builds confidence that these models lean on evidence genuinely tied to the classes.

ResNet50 behaves otherwise. For all its accuracy, its Grad-CAM maps are diffuse and its SHAP attributions weak or scattered over the background. Since it also predicts ``player'' everywhere, the explanations confirm that its accuracy springs from no real visual separation of the four roles.

The case is stronger because the two methods are built differently. Grad-CAM rides the gradients and internal activations; SHAP estimates contributions by masking the input. When such distinct techniques converge on the same pattern, it is unlikely to be a quirk of either one~\cite{nazir2023survey}.

The lesson: a high aggregate metric is no proof of sound reasoning. Here, explainability is not decoration but part of the evaluation --- it catches the classifier that shines in the numbers yet rests on inadequate evidence.

The explanations still demand caution. Grad-CAM has limited spatial resolution, born from deep maps and then upscaled; SHAP hinges on how regions are masked and on the reference used to replace parts of the image. So we treat them as complementary evidence, not as definitive proof of causality. In refereeing, commercial analysis, or sports decision-making, that verification is essential --- before trusting a model, one must check that its predictions rest on relevant regions and that its errors do not betray a reliance on shortcuts or background.

\subsection{Efficiency and Practical Deployment}

RQ5 yields a clear practical verdict. Many vision problems pit accuracy against efficiency: bigger models bring more capacity but also more memory and inference cost. Here that tension softened, because the lightest model also took the best macro F1-score.

The custom CNN has only 0.46 million parameters and 5.4 MB on disk --- small enough for common hardware, edge devices, or even web inference --- and its macro F1-score topped the transfer models, signalling better balance across classes on test. ResNet50, by contrast, weighs 147 MB across 24.8 million parameters. The highest overall accuracy bought no gain in per-class reliability: collapsed onto the player class, its extra cost returned no proportional advantage for this task. MobileNetV2 occupies the middle, larger than the custom CNN but far below ResNet50, at 3.05 million parameters and 30 MB, and it earns interest where pre-trained features help --- notably under blur or compression, where it showed some stability.

Deployment, even so, would still need human supervision. Goalkeeper stayed hard for the discriminative models, and errors there skew positioning analysis and tactical reading; input quality, too, bears directly on real performance whenever objects appear small, distant, or blurred. The ResNet50 case carries the sharpest operational warning of all: a system judged only by accuracy can look fine in an initial test and then fail silently in production, labelling almost everything ``player''. Responsible deployment, therefore, must weigh macro F1-score, per-class performance, robustness, and explainability --- not accuracy alone.

\subsection{Comparison with Existing Literature}

The study confirms something the imbalanced-learning literature already warns about: aggregate accuracy is an unsafe criterion for picking models. Here ResNet50 won on accuracy and lost on macro F1-score, which carries that warning into role classification for football images and shows that per-class metrics are indispensable in this domain~\cite{ghosh2024imbalance}.

The findings also echo transfer-learning comparisons on small datasets, where lightweight networks match or beat deeper architectures given little data and proper regularisation, augmentation, and learning-rate control~\cite{martins2025mobilenet}. The custom CNN outscored the larger models on macro F1-score, and MobileNetV2 stayed above ResNet50 on the same metric.

What sets this apart from much sports vision is the framing of the task. Prior work usually folds role identification into larger pipelines of detection, tracking, or re-identification~\cite{giancola2018soccernet,somers2024multitask}; here it stands alone, with its own evaluation, explainability, and robustness test.

The numerical comparison, again, deserves care. Datasets, splits, metrics, and goals all differ --- many works report mAP or tracking metrics, while we report accuracy, macro F1-score, and per-class performance on already-extracted crops. The results, then, are no claim of direct superiority. The real contribution is the integrated protocol: a leakage-free split, balancing confined to training, a controlled three-model comparison, Grad-CAM and SHAP, and a corruption-based robustness analysis --- together a fuller way to evaluate football role classifiers, beholden to no single aggregate metric.

\subsection{Practical and Scientific Contributions}

\textbf{Scientific Contributions.}
The work delivers a systematic, controlled comparison of a custom CNN trained from scratch against two transfer-learning backbones, MobileNetV2 and ResNet50, all under the same data, preprocessing, training protocol, and metrics --- the condition for fairly reading the differences between architectures.

A second contribution is the reliability analysis through explainability. Grad-CAM and SHAP together pinpointed when a model used object-linked regions and when it leaned on uninformative patterns; for ResNet50 they exposed the majority-class shortcut that accuracy alone hid. The robustness analysis adds to this: by corrupting the test set under control, the study showed that a model's apparent stability can mask degenerate behaviour, while the per-class error analysis named the roles that stay hard --- goalkeeper above all.

Finally, the study offers a reproducible recipe for turning a detection dataset into a role-classification benchmark. The core scientific message is simple: under strong imbalance, macro F1-score, per-class metrics, and visual explanations must be read together --- no single one of them measures reliability on its own.

\textbf{Practical Contributions.}
In practice, the work shows a compact model can outdo a larger one when data is scarce: the custom CNN posted the best macro F1-score while being the smallest, cheapest to store, and easiest to deploy. It also stands as a warning --- a high-accuracy model can be silently degenerate, as ResNet50 was when it labelled every crop ``player'', a failure that would slip past any evaluation built on accuracy alone.

Beyond that, the pipeline is a low-cost option for clubs, analysts, and researchers with limited resources, usable as a triage or pre-annotation tool that trims part of the manual work of classifying elements in football images. The human, though, stays in the loop: the predictions support analysts, they do not replace human review --- least of all in difficult cases or decisions with real sporting weight.

\subsection{Ethical, Social, and Safety Implications}

The task here is classifying on-pitch roles, not identifying individuals, which makes it less sensitive than facial recognition or the nominal tracking of athletes. Still, the broadcast images show real people in a public context, and any push toward individual identification would raise questions of privacy, consent, and data use.

A second ethical concern is the uneven reliability across classes. Some roles are recognised more confidently than others --- player beat goalkeeper in the discriminative models --- so a decision resting on a goalkeeper prediction is less trustworthy than one resting on a player prediction. Used carelessly, that gap causes real trouble: in performance analysis, class-specific errors distort statistics and tactical reads; near refereeing, the stakes are higher, since a wrong prediction can sway a sensitive call.

There is also the trap of false confidence. ResNet50 would look reliable under accuracy alone, yet its predictions had degenerated to the majority class --- in a real system, exactly the kind of behaviour that breeds undue trust in an output that never distinguishes the roles.

For all this, the framework is decision support, not an autonomous system. Its unsupervised use is not advised, especially in high-risk settings, and anything tied to refereeing, formal assessment, or weighty sports decisions should keep human verification mandatory.

\subsection{Limitations}

The study carries real limitations. The first is the dataset's size and origin: 663 images from a single public source, which curbs how far the results generalise to other competitions, broadcasters, stadiums, camera angles, and broadcast conditions.

The second is the imbalance. The 15,636 crops notwithstanding, the minority classes have few examples, especially in test --- and with ball and goalkeeper so sparse, their per-class metrics rest on small samples and should be read with caution.

The design adds its own caveats. Each model was trained once and evaluated on a single split, so small differences between models came without statistical validation, confidence intervals, or multi-seed tests. We ran no external validation on an independent dataset, and the hyperparameter search was bounded by a single GPU. The results, then, are a controlled comparison within fixed conditions --- not an exhaustive optimisation of each architecture.

Finally, the system evaluated in this work does not perform object detection on complete frames. It classifies crops already extracted from annotated boxes. In a complete application, the performance would also depend on the quality of an external detector or localiser.

These limitations set the scope of the evidence. They do not invalidate the results --- they mark which parts of the conclusion to read with care.

\subsection{Future Research Directions}

The clearest next step is to expand and diversify the dataset. Larger, more balanced collections --- with many more minority examples, goalkeeper first of all --- would give a far better read on how the models generalise, and external data from other leagues, broadcasters, stadiums, and camera setups would test that generalisation honestly.

Statistical soundness needs strengthening too. Repeated runs with different seeds, confidence intervals, and significance tests would separate genuine differences between models from the noise of a single training run.

A natural move is to fold the classifier into an end-to-end system, coupling it with an object detector such as a YOLO-family model so it works directly on full frames rather than pre-annotated crops~\cite{liang2025basketball} --- a step that brings the system closer to real sports-video analysis.

Other avenues remain open. Efficient backbones such as EfficientNet could be paired with imbalance-aware losses like focal loss, and uncertainty estimation would let the system abstain on ambiguous or low-quality crops. Explainability can go deeper as well: comparing Grad-CAM and SHAP maps with judgements from football or computer-vision experts would test whether the highlighted regions make sense to human eyes.

Finally, the practical side deserves a real trial --- inference time, memory, and performance on constrained devices, measured against data captured from varied, genuine broadcasts.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

This work tackled the automatic classification of four roles in football images --- ball, goalkeeper, player, and referee --- through a comparative, explainable CNN framework that pitted a lightweight custom CNN against MobileNetV2 and ResNet50 on crops from a public dataset. The original split was preserved to curb leakage, balancing touched only training, and the models were read through per-class metrics, Grad-CAM, SHAP, and robustness tests under five corruptions.

The headline finding is that the highest accuracy did not mark the best model. ResNet50 reached 84.0\% on test but collapsed to the majority class, scoring just 0.23 macro F1. The custom CNN, with a mere 0.46 million parameters, was the most balanced of all, at 77.9\% accuracy and 0.67 macro F1.

Grad-CAM and SHAP backed this up. For the custom CNN and MobileNetV2, the explanations fell on the objects --- the players' bodies, the ball; for ResNet50 they were diffuse and barely tied to the object. The robustness analysis caught the same pathology: ResNet50's numbers stayed frozen across every corruption because it kept predicting ``player'' regardless of the input.

The practical takeaway is that a smaller, cheaper model can be the more reliable and more deployable one in resource-constrained settings --- though human supervision stays necessary, not least because goalkeeper remained hard for the discriminative models. The chief limitation is the small, single-source, imbalanced dataset evaluated on a single split, which points to the obvious next move: a larger, better-balanced dataset, richer in goalkeeper examples, validated on independent broadcasts.
